title: Saffir–Simpson scale
wiki_lead:
The Saffir–Simpson hurricane wind scale (SSHWS) is a tropical cyclone intensity scale that classifies hurricanes—which in the Western Hemisphere are tropical cyclones that exceed the intensities of tropical depressions and tropical storms—into five categories distinguished by the intensities of their sustained winds. This measuring system was formerly known as the Saffir–Simpson hurricane scale, or SSHS.
To be classified as a hurricane, a tropical cyclone must have one-minute-average maximum sustained winds at 10 m (33 ft) above the surface of at least 74 mph (64 kn, 119 km/h; Category 1). The highest classification in the scale, Category 5, consists of storms with sustained winds of at least 157 mph (137 kn, 252 km/h). The classifications can provide some indication of the potential damage and flooding a hurricane will cause upon landfall.
The Saffir–Simpson hurricane wind scale is based on the highest wind speed averaged over a one-minute interval 10 m above the surface. Although the scale shows wind speeds in continuous speed ranges, the US National Hurricane Center and the Central Pacific Hurricane Center assign tropical cyclone intensities in 5-knot (kn) increments (e.g., 100, 105, 110, 115 kn, etc.) because of the inherent uncertainty in estimating the strength of tropical cyclones. Wind speeds in knots are then converted to other units and rounded to the nearest 5 mph or 5 km/h.
The Saffir–Simpson hurricane wind scale is used officially only to describe hurricanes that form in the Atlantic Ocean and northern Pacific Ocean east of the International Date Line. Other areas use different scales to label these storms, which are called cyclones or typhoons, depending on the area. These areas (except the JTWC) use three-minute or ten-minute averaged winds to determine the maximum sustained wind speed, creating an important difference which frustrates direct comparison between maximum wind speeds of storms measured using the Saffir–Simpson hurricane wind scale (usually 14% more intense) and those measured using a ten-minute interval (usually 12% less intense).
There is some criticism of the SSHWS for not accounting for rain, storm surge, and other important factors, but SSHWS defenders say that part of the goal of SSHWS is to be straightforward and simple to understand. There have been proposals for the addition of higher categories to the scale, which would then set a maximum cutoff for Category 5, but none have been adopted as of October 2025.

History
In 1971, the scale was developed by civil engineer Herbert Saffir and meteorologist Robert Simpson, who at the time was director of the U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC). In 1973, the scale was introduced to the general public, and saw widespread use after Neil Frank replaced Simpson at the helm of the NHC in 1974.

grok_lead: The SaffirâSimpson Hurricane Wind Scale is a five-category classification system that rates tropical cyclones, specifically hurricanes in the Atlantic Ocean and the northeastern Pacific Ocean, based solely on their maximum sustained wind speeds measured as 1-minute averages at 10 meters above the surface. Developed to estimate potential property damage from hurricane winds, the scale ranges from Category 1 (74â95 mph or 119â153 km/h) for minimal hurricanes to Category 5 (157 mph or 252 km/h or higher) for catastrophic ones, with Categories 3 through 5 designated as "major" hurricanes capable of causing devastating structural impacts. It does not account for other hazards such as storm surge, rainfall-induced flooding, or tornadoes, which can significantly amplify overall destruction. The scale was originally conceived in the late 1960s and early 1970s by American structural engineer Herbert Saffir, who developed it as part of a guide for minimum building standards in hurricane-prone areas, and Robert H. Simpson, then-director of the National Hurricane Center (NHC), who adapted it for meteorological forecasting purposes. Saffir's contribution focused on engineering assessments of wind damage to structures, while Simpson integrated it into public warnings to communicate storm intensity more effectively; the scale was developed in 1971 and adopted for operational use by the NHC in 1975. Initially known simply as the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Scale, it included estimates of central pressure and storm surge heights alongside wind speeds, but these were removed in a 2010 update by the NHC to emphasize that the rating reflects wind hazards only, renaming it the SaffirâSimpson Hurricane Wind Scale. In practice, the scale guides emergency preparedness, evacuation decisions, and infrastructure planning by describing expected wind impacts: Category 1 storms may cause minor roof and tree damage with power outages lasting hours to days; Category 2 brings extensive roof and siding failures with outages potentially lasting weeks; Category 3 results in widespread destruction of mobile homes, roofs, and vegetation; Category 4 leads to severe structural failures in well-built homes and long-term utility disruptions; and Category 5 can completely destroy most residences and infrastructure, rendering areas uninhabitable for months. Officially maintained by the National Hurricane Center under the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the scale applies only to hurricanes achieving at least 74 mph sustained winds and remains a cornerstone of tropical cyclone communication despite calls for expansions, such as a potential Category 6 for winds exceeding 192 mph, amid intensifying storms linked to climate change.
